question: Will the 'Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act' be formally introduced in Congress by September 18, 2026?

calls.reasoning: Status quo is NO: as of 2026-09-07 the bill is announced but unfiled, and Sanders's own release calls it 'forthcoming legislation' they 'will introduce'. The decisive structural fact is the calendar — Senate returns 2026-09-14 after a long August/September state work period, House votes resume 2026-09-14 after a district work period the week of Sept 7. So essentially all probability mass sits in the 5 session days Sept 14-18, plus a small tail for hopper/pro-forma or already-quietly-filed. Reference class: high-profile 'forthcoming legislation' press rollouts by senior members, where introduction almost always follows (~85-90%) but the median lag is 1-4 weeks. Pulling up: the summary PDF already quotes statutory-sounding definitional text (drafting looks advanced), the announcement was timed to a news hook while the Senate was out, and the obvious plan is to file on return; either chamber alone suffices. Pulling down: the natural forcing function is the pre-midterm target adjournment (~early October), which sits AFTER Sept 18, so the window captures only the first of roughly three available session weeks; Sept 14-30 staff bandwidth is consumed by the funding-deadline fight; and Casar did not file on Sept 3-4 when the House was in session, which is consistent with text not being final. Could not verify from Congress.gov directly (403), a real limitation.

Bernie Sanders... introduced legislation Thursday' but cites NO S. or H.R. number and links only to the press release — loose usage of 'introduced' is widespread in this coverage (several outlet headlines say 'introduces bill'; the sponsor's own language says 'forthcoming').
- As of 2026-09-07, no report dated Sept 4-7 carries an assigned bill number for this title.
- CALENDAR (Senate): per Roll Call's writeup of the released 2026 Senate calendar, the Senate stayed in session the first week of August 'but then won't return until Sept. 14.'
- CALENDAR (House): per the same source and the House 2026 calendar, the House held a one-week session beginning Aug 31 (which included Sept 3-4), then a district work period the week of Sept 7; next votes Monday Sept 14.
- Consequence: within the remaining window, both chambers are in session only Sept 14-18 (5 session days). Note as procedure, not prediction: House members can drop bills in the hopper during pro forma sessions, and the Senate commonly permits bill introduction during adjournment by unanimous consent order — so recess filing is procedurally possible.
- Neither sponsor filed during Sept 3-4 while the House WAS in session and Casar was available to file.
- Competing floor context: FY2027 government funding deadline is Sept 30, 2026, so Sept 14-30 floor and staff time is dominated by appropriations. Bill introduction itself consumes no floor time.
- Election-year context: 2026 is a midterm year; the target adjournment for campaigning is early October, i.e. AFTER the Sept 18 deadline — the sponsors' own natural filing deadline sits outside this question's window.
- Sponsor characteristics: Sanders is a prolific introducer of messaging legislation and does not require cosponsors to file. Casar is the House lead. Bicameral simultaneous introduction was the announced framing.
- Substance context: bill is far-reaching (permanent superintelligence ban, pause on frontier development, new cabinet-level agency, 20-year prison terms, corporate dissolution), announced the same day OpenAI's 'GPT-6 Astra' release was framed as AGI arrival and after reported summer rogue-AI-agent incidents. Public criticism already registered (e.g., Gary Marcus opposing; Science.org piece on experts disagreeing on the term 'superintelligence').

Constructed anchor, stated as such: over the class of press-released 'forthcoming legislation' by senior members, eventual formal introduction is the strong majority outcome (roughly 85-90%); conditional on NOT filing on the announcement day, introduction within the FIRST subsequent session week is roughly a coin flip, with the remainder spread over the following weeks and a residual that never files under the announced title. Treat these as reasoned estimates, not sourced statistics.
- Conditional refinement worth carrying: the relevant conditioning variable here is 'the sponsors' chamber was out of session on announcement day and returns mid-window,' which concentrates any filing into Sept 14-18 rather than spreading it uniformly across the 15 calendar days.

Eventual introduction under the announced title runs ~85-90%; the binding constraint here is timing, not intent. The announcement (2026-09-03) fell in a recess: the Senate returns 2026-09-14 (Roll Call 2026 calendar) and the House's next votes are 2026-09-14, so the only realistic in-window opportunity is the single week of Sept 14-18, with roughly three session weeks (Sept 14-18, Sept 21-25, Sept 28-Oct 2) available before both chambers leave for nearly all of October in this election year. Cutting against: only a summary was released, not text, and a bill creating a cabinet-level agency plus 20-year criminal penalties is a heavy Legislative Counsel draft; Casar had House floor days Sept 3-4 and chose announcement over filing; the return week is consumed by the Sept 30 funding deadline. Runs 1 and 3 diluted their estimates across three phantom session weeks. (b) whether a Sept 30 funding fight crowds out September - CHECKED and settled AGAINST Runs 1 and 3: a stopgap through Dec 11 was signed Sept 2, and that is precisely why the weeks were cut; the crowd-out argument is void.
